text:
A: Hiya! Can you hear me okay?
B: Yeah. I'm Gemma.
A: Blerta. I'm in Newcastle. You're Nottingham, is it? Kezia might've said.
B: Sutton-in-Ashfield. Near enough.
A: Sorry, I've already got it wrong. What do you do?
B: Manage a builders' merchants. You're a student, are you? I saw the hoodie.
A: Yeah, second year. Speech and language therapy. I'm a bit older than most of them, I'm twenty-seven.
B: Speech therapy. Is that like after a stroke and that?
A: Yeah, that's the bit I want to do, actually. Adults. Stroke and dementia. Why, do you know someone?
B: My dad. Had one last year.
A: Oh, I'm sorry. How's he getting on?
B: Better. His words came back, mostly. But he gets stuck. He knows what he wants and it won't come out, and then he gets mardy, and then my mum gets mardy with him.
A: That's really, really common. It's called word-finding difficulty. It's not him being awkward, it's like the word's on a shelf he can see but can't reach.
B: That's what he says. Not in them words. He says it's on the tip of his tongue all day.
A: Yeah. One thing that sometimes helps families is, erm, not jumping in with the word straight away. Give him a few seconds. And if he can't get it, ask him to describe it. Like, what's it for, what colour is it. Sorry, I don't want to tell you what to do.
B: No, that's useful. Mum finishes all his sentences. Drives him up the wall.
A: My mam does that to my dad and he hasn't even had a stroke!
B: Ha. Lee does it to me.
A: Is he still getting therapy, your dad?
B: Had some. Then it stopped. Waiting list, I think. Nobody's said owt.
A: You can ask the GP to re-refer, sometimes. It's worth asking. Honestly, they don't always tell you.
B: Right. I'll get mum to ring. Or I'll ring. She won't.
A: What's he like, your dad? Like, before?
B: Pit man. Worked down the colliery till it shut. Loud. Never shut up. So it's strange, him stuck for words.
A: That must be hard to watch.
B: It's fine. Well. It's not fine. But you get on with it.
A: Yeah. I worked in a care home six years, I saw a lot of families get on with it. You look after yourself as well, though.
B: I walk the dog. That's me looking after myself.
A: That counts! I walk on the Town Moor. Clears your head. What's your dog—
